sections.h2: Where is Laurel, Maryland, and how is the city laid out?
sections.html:
Laurel is a city in Prince George's County, Maryland, on the Patuxent River between Washington, D.C. and Baltimore. It is part of the Washington metropolitan area and sits on the fall line of the river, which is why mills once lined its banks.

The city is split into two wards. Ward 1 lies north of MD 198 and Ward 2 lies south of it. The mayor serves a four-year term, and the council has five members.

A Laurel mailing address does not always mean a Laurel city address. The city's own tax page warns that ZIP codes 20707 and 20708 may fall in the county instead of the city, and that 20723 is Howard County and 20724 is Anne Arundel County. Before you assume city rules apply to your house, check the parcel.

sections.h2: What is the history behind Laurel's older homes?
sections.html:
Laurel began as a mill town. The Snowden family patented the land in 1658, Nicholas Snowden built a grist mill around 1811, and the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad arrived in 1835. The community was first called Laurel Factory, and the town was incorporated in 1870.

Mill workers' housing, a school and shops grew up around the cotton mills. As manufacturing faded in the late 1800s, Laurel turned into a commuter suburb. The Laurel Park racetrack opened in 1911 and still runs thoroughbred racing.

In 1975 a historic district was created around Main Street. That matters to a seller because older houses in the northern part of the city can carry design review rules, covered below.

sections.h2: What do the surrounding areas around Laurel look like?
sections.html:
Several named areas touch the city, and buyers and sellers use these names loosely. The census-designated areas around Laurel include:

  • West Laurel and South Laurel in Prince George's County
  • North Laurel in Howard County
  • Maryland City in Anne Arundel County
  • Konterra, a large development on land that was once part of Laurel

The Grove is a historically African American neighborhood, and the Main Street historic district is the town's center. MD 198 divides the two wards.

sections.h2: Who lives and works in Laurel, and how do residents get around?
sections.html:
Laurel is mostly residential. Population grew from 19,960 in 2000 to 25,115 in 2010 and 30,060 in 2020, and the median age in 2020 was 35.2.

Employers in and around Laurel include the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, which has a Laurel address and a campus in Howard County, the University of Maryland Laurel Medical Center, and the racetrack. Many residents commute to Washington or Baltimore.

Getting around is easier than in much of the county:

  • MARC Laurel Station is on the Camden Line between Baltimore and Washington. A second station, Laurel Race Track, sits just north of the city limits.
  • Metrobus and RTA buses serve the city, including the 87 Laurel Express.
  • U.S. 1, MD 198, Interstate 95 and the Baltimore-Washington Parkway all pass through or beside Laurel.

Those transit links are worth listing when you describe the house to any buyer.

Public schools in Laurel are run by Prince George's County Public Schools. The neighborhood high school is Laurel High School and the middle school is Dwight D. Eisenhower Middle. Elementary schools named for the area include Bond Mill, Deerfield Run, James H. Harrison, Laurel, Montpelier, Oaklands and Scotchtown Hills.

Families also look at CMIT Academy North, a charter school, and private options such as St. Vincent Pallotti High School and St. Mary of the Mills School. The Laurel College Center is shared by Prince George's Community College and Howard Community College.

sections.h2: How does Laurel's weather affect a house?
sections.html:
Laurel has a humid subtropical climate: a July average high near 88 degrees, a January average low near 25 degrees, about 47 inches of rain and about 11 inches of snow a year.

Two past events show what the area can produce. Hurricane Agnes caused record flooding across Maryland in June 1972, and an F3-level tornado hit Laurel on September 24, 2001. Because the city sits along the Patuxent River, a house near the water deserves a closer look at drainage and basement moisture before it is listed or inspected.

The city also expects owners to deal with snow quickly. Its code requires snow to be cleared within 12 hours after it stops and ice within 12 hours after it forms.

sections.h2: What city rules should a Laurel seller check first?
sections.html:
The first thing to check is whether the house has an open code violation, a rental license problem or a historic district rule attached to it. Each of these can slow a conventional sale.

  • Correction orders. The city issues a correction order before a fine. For vehicles, grass and weeds, and trash and debris it generally allows three days. Grass and weeds cannot exceed 8 inches, and unregistered or inoperable vehicles cannot be kept on a driveway. If an order is ignored, the city can do the work and place a lien.
  • Rental license. Owners of rental units need a license at $40 per unit per year. Properties with fewer than 12 units are inspected every three years, and new participants get an initial inspection.
  • Foreclosure notice. When a foreclosure is filed on residential property in the city, written notice goes to the city within five calendar days from the person authorized to make the sale.
  • Historic district. The Laurel historic district is made up of seven contiguous districts in the north of the city. Changes to a structure need a Certificate of Approval, and removing a tree visible from the street can need approval too.

The city's Fire Marshal and Permit Services office handles licensing and inspections at 301-725-5300.

sections.h2: How does property tax work for a Laurel house?
sections.html:
A Laurel city homeowner pays one consolidated bill that Prince George's County issues, and it includes the city's tax. The city charges $0.71 per $100 of assessed value, and the county's fiscal 2026 real property rate is $1.0000 per $100 before its special rates.

If a lender pays from escrow, the owner is still responsible, so confirm after any refinance or loan transfer. For questions about balances, call the city Budget and Personnel Services office at 301-725-5300, extension 2248.

Sale costs also include transfer tax. The state guide on local taxing authority says Prince George's County's transfer tax is capped at 1.4% and that a 1% rate applies to certain principal residence sales to county classroom teachers and police officers. Your settlement company can tell you the rate on your closing.

sections.h2: What do Laurel sellers usually face, and where does a cash sale fit?
sections.html:
Sellers in Laurel most often face a house that is older, rented, inherited or behind on code or tax items. Those are the situations where preparing a listing costs more time than the owner has.

A cash purchase skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting steps, so the buyer can close on the owner's schedule and take the house as it stands. It does not remove the need to clear liens, resolve a rental license or confirm who has authority to sell an inherited property. Ask any buyer, in writing, how those items will be handled before you sign.

If you are comparing routes, line up three numbers: what a listing would net after repairs and sale costs, how many months of carrying costs you can absorb, and what a written cash offer would net. The comparison is usually clearer than a general rule about which route is better.

faqs.q: Is Laurel, MD in Prince George's County?
faqs.a: Yes. The City of Laurel is in Prince George's County, though nearby addresses with a Laurel mailing address can sit in Howard County or Anne Arundel County. Check the parcel before assuming county or city rules.

faqs.q: When are Laurel property taxes due?
faqs.a: Real property tax is billed in July and due September 30, with a semi-annual option for owner-occupied homes of 50% by September 30 and 50% by December 31. Payments after September 30 carry 1.667% a month.

faqs.q: Do I need a rental license to sell a rented house in Laurel?
faqs.a: The license applies to owners of rental units in the city, at $40 per unit per year, with an inspection for new participants. The city page does not say how a license changes hands in a sale, so call 301-725-5300 before closing.

faqs.q: Can the city fine me for tall grass or a junk vehicle before I sell?
faqs.a: Yes. Laurel issues a correction order first, generally with three days to fix grass over 8 inches, trash or an unregistered vehicle. If it goes unfixed, the city can do the work at your cost, add a lien or levy fines.

faqs.q: Does the Laurel historic district affect selling?
faqs.a: It can. Houses in the seven contiguous districts in the north of the city need a Certificate of Approval for changes to the structure, and tree removal visible from the street can need approval. A buyer planning repairs should check this first.
